$comment: Pinned bounds for the creation census. EVERY value carries a stated reason in `justification`, keyed `<group>.<key>`, and test/creation-census.test.ts fails if one is missing or a stub. 'No measurement backs this, and here is what would' is an acceptable reason; inventing an anchor is not.

census.savedQueryName: slot-zero: creation census - deployers creating in one month (COHORT_SQL)

justification.dune.monthlyCreditCapCredits: THE CAPTAIN'S OWN MONTHLY CEILING, IN CONFIGURATION BECAUSE THAT IS THE ONLY PLACE IT MAY LIVE. Captain decision 322a, 2026-08-06: 4,000 credits a month, not to be exceeded and not to be left unspent either. NOT A MEASUREMENT: it is the operator's stated budget, so this entry names its source rather than an anchor. THE SAME NUMBER UNDER THE SAME KEY IS PINNED IN tools/deployer-screen/thresholds.json -> dune.monthlyCreditCapCredits, and test/dune-credit-ceiling.test.ts pins the two equal — neither keyed tool may import the other, so one number across both is a duplicated value held together by a test, exactly as the credit guard's own text is. An operator changing the cap changes BOTH. HOW IT BINDS: client.mjs -> bindingCreditCeiling takes the SMALLER of this and the vendor's reported credits_included for the current billing period, and decideAllowance measures that period's own credits_used against it — which enforces a monthly total on a tool that holds no state between runs, since the vendor's counter is the ACCOUNT's running total rather than a run's. Both figures reach every verdict, so a refusal states which ceiling bound and whether raising the cap or waiting for the period to roll is the fix. WHAT IT ENFORCES IS PER ACCOUNT-PERIOD RATHER THAN FLEET-WIDE: the fleet holds more than one Dune key, separate keys are separate accounts with their own quotas and their own period boundaries, and each counter sees only its own spend, so two keys each honouring this cap spend twice it between them. Closing that needs one key or a smaller cap on each, and both are the captain's decision. NO VENDOR FIGURE OR PERIOD IS WRITTEN DOWN HERE: the guard reads both live from whichever key this lane's credential resolves to. This lane DEFERS rather than falling back when a ceiling refuses it — it has no keyless substitute for the enumeration.
justification.census.queryId: The saved Dune query holding COHORT_SQL, deployed 2026-08-04 by `run.mjs --deploy --live` under captain decision 187a. `null` before deployment rather than a guessed id, so nothing can execute the wrong statement under this name. IT WAS RECORDED AS UNDEPLOYABLE AND THAT WAS FALSE: `tools/arrival-rate-walk/cohort.mjs`, that lane's README and CLAUDE.md all said the Free tier's ten private query slots were full and the account held ten. The account held EIGHT, six of them retired scratch probes, and the stale sentence is why this widening sat undone for a month. Do not replace it with another number to be taken on faith: the count is re-checkable at any time with `GET https://api.dune.com/api/v1/queries?limit=100` (header `X-Dune-API-Key`), whose `total` field is the figure, and `run.mjs --deploy` counts it itself immediately before creating anything and refuses rather than asserting.
justification.census.savedQueryName: The name the deploy step gives the saved query. It says which repository constant the text came from, because the account is shared with scratch probes and a query whose provenance is not in its own name is one a later reader has to diff to identify. It is not load-bearing: the text is what is verified, byte for byte, before every execution.
justification.census.defaultMonth: 2026-07, the month captain decision 187a's own case is measured on: the current feed sees 25 deployers creating in it against the census's 10,280, and at the Stage 1 competence gate 8 against 35 - the 27 named wallets this project structurally could not see (`data/slot-zero-discovery-widen-operations/report.md` sections 2.1 and 4.1). It is also the month whose deployers are screenable TODAY, which is what the captain's question asks about ('can I beat the dev ... currently'). NOTE THE OTHER LANE'S MONTH IS DIFFERENT AND DELIBERATELY SO: `tools/arrival-rate-walk/bounds.json` seeds from 2026-01 because it needs forward OBSERVATION time, not current relevance, and widening there goes backwards. One census month is one execution, so serving both is a second run rather than a compromise.
justification.census.minLaunches: 30 creations in the seed month. IT IS A PROLIFIC-NESS CUT, NOT A COMPETENCE ONE - `census.mjs` -> PROLIFIC_CUT_CAVEAT is the sentence and it travels to the record, the rendered summary and the README. It selects on volume in one past month and on nothing else: no bonding rate, no completion, no 'still active' term, so it carries no survivorship bias, unlike the vendor feed's filter which looked like quality and was tempo. What it DOES miss is the low-cadence deployer, invisibly. The VALUE is chosen for result size rather than for meaning: the measured ladder for 2026-07 is 10,280 deployers at >=8, 5,416 at >=15 and 3,036 at >=30, and 3,036 rows at the ~100 bytes/row this repo has measured is ~0.3 MB, about 6 export credits against a 2,500-credit monthly free tier. A floor of 8 would be ~17 credits for the same answer plus a longer tail nothing downstream can walk. Tuning the sample SIZE is legitimate and is disclosed here; tuning it to reach a finding is not, and nothing in this lane reads the result before choosing.
justification.census.maxRows: 5,000 deployer rows per result, and the unit that matters is BYTES: Dune bills results at ~20 credits/MB and retrieving them is ~71% of the bill. At the measured 3,036 qualifying deployers for 2026-07 at the pinned floor, 5,000 is ~65% headroom - enough that a month running heavier than the probe does not truncate, and low enough that the read stays a single-digit-credit one. A result that DOES hit the cap is refused rather than published: the SQL carries the qualifying count before the cap as its own row, so truncation is detected exactly, and the surviving rows would be the most prolific ones, which is a selection rather than a shortfall.
justification.census.maxRowsCeiling: 20,000, the ceiling `--max-rows` may not be raised past from the command line. It is roughly the whole free tier's monthly export budget in one read (20,000 rows at ~100 bytes/row is ~2 MB, ~40 credits), so a census larger than this is a decision about the month's allowance rather than a flag on one run. A run now PRICES itself against the period's remaining credits before it spends (`dune.allowanceRequired` and README.md -> 'The monthly credit ceiling'), but NOTHING HERE TRACKS THE PERIOD ACROSS RUNS - the tool is stateless between them - which is exactly why the per-run ceiling has to be a real one.
justification.census.resultLimitHeadroom: 64 rows added to `max_rows` when the result is read. The `?limit=` must sit STRICTLY above the largest result the SQL can produce or a complete result reads as one truncated at its own limit and is refused - the read's own wholeness check treats rows-equal-to-limit as unprovable. The SQL returns at most `max_rows` deployer rows plus its coverage and total rows, so 64 covers today's three meta rows with room for a probe row a later version adds. It costs nothing: the limit bounds the read, the SQL bounds the result.
justification.dune.maxExecutionsPerRun: 1. AN EXECUTION IS BILLED WHETHER OR NOT IT SUCCEEDS AND IS NEVER RETRIED, and one census month is one execution by construction - the coverage probe rides in the same result as the count rather than costing a second one. A run that could spend two executions could spend two bills for one answer, so the ceiling is the design rather than a safety margin. Captain decision 187a authorised one census month at low single-digit credits; this is that bound in code.
justification.dune.maxRequestsPerRun: 48 requests of every kind, and the number is DERIVED rather than chosen: the ceiling must COVER a whole successful run, which is 1 credit-guard POST /usage + 1 saved-query verification + 1 execution POST + up to `dune.maxPollAttempts` status polls + 1 result read, plus headroom for `getJson`'s single 5xx/transport retry. That is `maxPollAttempts + 5` and this value must never sit below it - RAISING `maxPollAttempts` WITHOUT RAISING THIS IS HALF A CHANGE. THE CANCEL IS THE ONE REQUEST THIS CEILING MAY NOT REFUSE and it is therefore NOT in that sum (captain decision 381): an abandonment happens with the request budget at or near its limit by construction, so a ceiling that blocked `client.mjs` -> `cancelExecution` would turn a bounded bill into an unbounded one at exactly the moment the bound is needed. It still counts as ISSUED, so a run that had to cancel reports `requests` one above this ceiling rather than the counter quietly under-reporting; a successful run never sends one. The failure it exists to prevent is the worst shape a metered surface has: at 40 the request ceiling bound first, so an execution completing on a late poll exhausted the budget BEFORE the result read and the run burned a billed, unrecoverable execution and then refused to read its own answer - the money is spent and the answer is thrown away. Requests are not the billed unit here (bytes and executions are), so above that floor this bounds only wall clock, a wedged poll loop and polite use of a shared host.
justification.dune.pollIntervalMs: 3,000 ms between status polls. NO MEASUREMENT BACKS THIS NUMBER, and here is what would: the distribution of this query's own execution time over several months, which does not exist until it has run several times. It is chosen against the screen's experience that a scan of these tables completes in tens of seconds, and a poll is a read - it costs no credits - so the interval trades a little latency for a shorter poll loop.
justification.dune.maxPollAttempts: 40 polls, so ~2 minutes of waiting at the pinned interval before the run gives up. It is deliberately larger than any execution this repository has measured, because timing out early on a slow-but-fine execution wastes the bill entirely. IT IS THE REQUEST BUDGET, NOT THE GIVE-UP POINT — `dune.executionDeadlineMs` is the give-up point and is the authority (captain decision 381), and this must COVER it: a test pins `maxPollAttempts x pollIntervalMs >= executionDeadlineMs`, so the request budget can never be what silently ends the wait first. GIVING UP IS NO LONGER FREE-AND-CHEAP AND THAT SENTENCE USED TO BE HERE: the old text said the execution 'is billed by then and is not retried', which was true and incomplete — the engine kept running to Dune's own 30-minute limit and billed the full limit, measured at 180.002 credits. Both give-up paths now CANCEL first. A later run can still read the saved query's cached result, which is why giving up remains recoverable.
justification.dune.minIntervalMs: 250 ms between request starts, the same pacing the screen's Dune client uses and for the same reason: this is a shared host and a free tier, and nothing in this lane is latency-sensitive. No shed event has been observed at it across either lane's runs.
justification.dune.worstCaseCreditsPerExecution: 200 credits, RAISED FROM 25 BY CAPTAIN DECISION 381 (2026-08-08) AND RE-DERIVED AGAINST THE ENGINE TIMEOUT RATHER THAN AGAINST THIS STATEMENT. It is the WORST case this census's single execution may cost, and the input the monthly-ceiling guard converts a plan into money with (client.mjs -> estimatePlanCredits). WHY THE OLD DERIVATION WAS THE WRONG QUANTITY: it priced what COHORT_SQL costs when it works. MEASURED 2026-08-03 for the neighbouring lane's queries over the same decoded create surfaces, enumeration 0.919 execution credits and coverage probe 0.751; this census's own committed run (runs/2026-07-census.json) read 188,232 bytes for 3,036 rows in one execution; the widest execution any slot-zero lane had recorded that does NOT join the trade tape was 19.25 credits, and the two that DID join `dex_solana.trades` cost 81.74 and 221.51 (`slot-zero-launch-venue-daily-rates` section 7, held in firstmate's records, not in this repo). All of that is still true and none of it bounds anything: a statement that DEGRADES — a table grows, a partition stops pruning, the planner picks a different join — does not cost a little more, it runs until Dune's engine kills it. MEASURED 2026-08-08: a statement that compiled, ran to the 30-minute engine limit, returned no rows and ended QUERY_STATE_FAILED billed 180.002 credits, read off the free POST /usage counter either side with no other execution in flight (219.825 -> 399.827) and re-read after settling (`slot-zero-venue-gradeability-inventory` -> report.md section 0, held in firstmate's records, not in this repo). That is 7.2x the old pin, and the guard cleared the plan that did it at a pinned 6. SO THE NUMBER IS DERIVED FROM THE VENDOR'S CEILING, NOT FROM OUR STATEMENT: client.mjs -> executionDeadlineCredits(ENGINE_TIMEOUT_MS) is 181 credits (180.002 rounded up to whole credits, which is the granularity the vendor's counter advances in), and 200 is that plus ~10% because the reading is n=1 on one engine size against a vendor that publishes no rate. A test pins this value at or above that floor, so it cannot drift back below it. WHAT IT DOES TO THIS CENSUS'S PLANNING, stated because it changes character rather than degree: the default plan's worst case goes 49.51 -> 224.51 credits (1 execution at 200, plus 2 reads x 5,064 rows x 121 B = 24.51 export), and at --max-rows 20000 it goes 122.11 -> 297.11. Against the 4,000-credit cap the run is REFUSED once the period's credits_used passes ~3,750 where it used to pass ~3,925, warns `tight` above ~3,526 (the reserve comes off the reading before the tight multiple is applied, exactly as it does for the refusal), and the period affords ~17 reserved default runs rather than ~80. On a key whose vendor plan is 2,500 the refusal moves to ~2,250. A REAL RUN IS NOWHERE NEAR IT — the committed run's own local estimate is ~5 credits — so what the raise costs is HEADROOM RESERVED, not credits spent, and refusing a census that would have cost 5 because it COULD have cost 224 is the direction this lane already fails in: a refused census costs nothing and can be re-run, while an execution that overruns cannot be taken back. THE PIN IS ONLY HALF THE ANSWER: `dune.executionDeadlineMs` is what actually caps a single execution, and a pin without the deadline reserves the money without bounding the spend. COHORT_SQL MAY NOT GROW A TRADE JOIN WITHOUT RE-MEASURING THIS NUMBER — the trade-join figures above sit under this pin, but they were successful executions and say nothing about where a joined statement's timeout floor is.
justification.dune.executionDeadlineMs: 120,000 ms — how long ONE execution may run before this client CANCELS it, captain decision 381 (2026-08-08). It is the half of that decision that bounds a spend rather than reserving against it: a pre-flight allowance check cannot cap an execution, because the spend happens after the check passes and Dune caps a single execution's cost nowhere. THE VALUE MOVES NOTHING TODAY AND THAT IS DELIBERATE: 120,000 is exactly `maxPollAttempts` 40 x `pollIntervalMs` 3,000, i.e. the give-up point this loop already had. What changes is what giving up MEANS — run.mjs -> executeAndRead now issues POST /execution/{id}/cancel before it refuses, where it used to walk away and leave the engine running on our money to the vendor's 30-minute limit. That is the measured failure: 180.002 credits for a result nobody read. THE TWO NUMBERS ARE ONE BOUND IN TWO UNITS AND THIS ONE IS THE AUTHORITY, which is captain decision 144a's rule (never write two numbers for a duration someone else controls); test/dune-credit-ceiling.test.ts pins `maxPollAttempts x pollIntervalMs >= executionDeadlineMs` so the request budget can never be what silently ends the wait first, and both give-up paths cancel so no path walks away from a live execution. WHAT THE DEFAULT IS WORTH IN CREDITS, because a lane's budget is sized from it: at the measured 180.002 credits per 30-minute timeout — ~6.0 credits an engine-minute, an INFERENCE from one reading, not a published rate — 120 s is at most 13 credits of compute (client.mjs -> executionDeadlineCredits, whole credits rounded up). CONDITIONALLY: cancelling bounds the WAIT for certain and the BILL only if Dune stops the engine on cancel, which the vendor does not document and settling would cost a deliberately-runaway execution. That is why `worstCaseCreditsPerExecution` stays at the ENGINE floor of 200 rather than dropping to 13 — the pin is honest under either answer, and the deadline is what makes 13 the expected worst case instead of 200. WHY 120 s IS CONSERVATIVE RATHER THAN TIGHT: it is 1/15 of the engine limit and >13x the longest Dune execution this repository has measured (6-9 s for the neighbouring lane's two queries, 2026-08-03). If COHORT_SQL ever needs longer, raise this and `worstCaseCreditsPerExecution` together and say what the extra engine time is worth.
justification.dune.resultBytesPerRowCeiling: 121 bytes per result row, the bound the credit guard multiplies the read limit by to price the EXPORT half of a run's worst case. MEASURED on this lane's own committed run: 188,232 bytes over 3,036 deployer rows is ~62 bytes/row, so 121 is ~2x the shape actually returned, and it is deliberately the same figure the screen pins for its wider six-column row rather than a tighter number of this lane's own — a census row is `deployer` plus a count, and one ceiling shared across both keyed lanes is one number to move when Dune changes how it serialises a result. It is a CEILING, not an estimate: the read is issued at `?limit=` census.maxRows + census.resultLimitHeadroom, so worst-case bytes are that limit x this x the reads a run may issue.
justification.dune.allowanceReserveCredits: 25 credits held back from every allowance reading before the plan is compared against it, and it exists because THE COUNTER LAGS. Measured on this account during the Dune evaluation: `credits_used` rose +6.0 while the evaluator was completely idle, and it lands in whole-credit jumps — so a reading understates spend, therefore OVERSTATES what remains, and a guard that spent to the last credit would be spending money the vendor has already taken. It also absorbs part of a gap it cannot measure, and the key being UNSHARED does not close it: the allowance is ONE ACCOUNT's, every lane and run of this fleet draws on the same account total, nothing tracks it between runs, so a sibling lane can spend between our reading and our execution — and a SEPARATE key is a separate account with its own quota and its own period, which a reading says nothing about. NO MEASUREMENT FIXES THE MULTIPLE and it is stated rather than dressed up: 25 is ~4x the single observed drift and 1% of the free tier's 2,500. What would justify a value: readings taken immediately before and after executions of known cost, which would price the lag distribution instead of one sample of it. The failure direction is the safe one — too large a reserve refuses a census that would have fitted, and a census refused before its execution costs nothing and can be re-run.
justification.dune.allowanceTightMultiple: 2. NOT A REFUSAL BAR — the threshold at which a run that WILL proceed prints a warning. A run whose worst case fits once but not twice may be the last one the period can afford, and an operator queueing heavier work behind it should learn that before the allowance is gone rather than from an HTTP 402 mid-run. NO MEASUREMENT BACKS THE 2, and here is what would: the distribution of Dune-spending runs per billing period, which does not exist because nothing here has yet run on a schedule. 2 is the smallest multiple that expresses 'this run is repeatable', which is the property that makes a failure recoverable.
justification.dune.allowanceRequired: `true` — the census REFUSES when POST /usage cannot be read, rather than executing blind. NOT A MEASUREMENT, a policy. An unreadable balance is not headroom, and 'we could not see it' is the same evidence as 'it is empty'. THIS LANE HAS NO FALLBACK — unlike the screen, which walks the Solana RPC when Dune refuses, a census with no Dune answer is no census — so the cost of refusing is one deferred run, while the cost of proceeding blind is a billed execution that returns nothing and cannot be retried this period. The reading itself is free (Dune documents /usage as a metadata endpoint consuming no credits) and is retried once, so a single transport hiccup does not reach this switch.
justification.dune.privateQuerySlots: 10, the Free tier's private-query allowance, which the deploy step counts the account against BEFORE creating anything. This number is the vendor's and can change; what makes the check honest is that the CURRENT usage is read live from `GET /api/v1/queries?limit=100` rather than asserted here. If the two disagree the deploy refuses and prints both, and it never deletes or archives an existing query to make room - which of them is retired is not this tool's call. MEASURED 2026-08-08 AND IT CONTRADICTS THIS PIN ON THE KEY THIS FLEET IS USING: `GET /queries?limit=100` reported `total: 0` and `POST /usage` reported `private_queries: 0`, yet `POST /api/v1/query` with `is_private: true` returned `402 {"error":"Max number of private queries reached"}` — i.e. the allowance on that account is ZERO, not ten, and creating a PUBLIC query succeeded instead (`slot-zero-venue-gradeability-inventory` -> report.md section 0, held in firstmate's records, not in this repo). CONSEQUENCE, STATED AND NOT ACTED ON: `run.mjs` -> `deploySavedQuery` sends `is_private: true`, so `--deploy --live` cannot succeed under that key — it will pass this local count and be refused by the vendor. The pin is LEFT AT 10 because it names the tier's allowance rather than this key's, the live count is what the check actually reads, and switching the deploy to a public query publishes the statement, which is a custody decision for the captain rather than a passing fix. Nothing is blocked by it today: query 8214953 is already deployed and every run VERIFIES rather than creates. A lane that needs a scratch slot on this key must create a PUBLIC query or it cannot run at all.
